title: Anger and Annoyance – Animals
description: Express degrees of anger and understand everyday animal idioms.

source.title: Advanced Grammar & Vocabulary — Express Publishing
source.note: Lesson vocabulary, examples and written tasks follow the supplied pages. Definitions are condensed for readability; spacing and obvious scan errors are corrected. Hints, explanations and model answers are study aids, not a publisher answer key.

lessons.title: Anger and annoyance
lessons.body: The document teaches both individual words and fixed expressions for anger. Learn the complete expression and the situation illustrated by its sentence. Livid in the anger sense is used after a verb, not normally before a noun.

lessons.title: Animal expressions
lessons.body: The animal section includes idioms and verbs. Pay attention to verb forms in the examples: dogged, ducked, hounded and rabbited. Use the meaning, not a literal translation of the animal.
terms: have a whale of a time

vocabulary.example: We had a blazing row.
vocabulary.note: Row rhymes with cow in this meaning.

vocabulary.example: When she told him, he blew his top and began shouting.
You'd better do what your teacher says, or she will get very cross.
I'm always a bit crotchety when I wake up in the mornings.
That constant drilling noise outside my house is driving me up the wall.
vocabulary.note: Informal; pronoun changes with the person.

vocabulary.example: When they told him, he was furious and left the room.
The most galling thing about his winning all that money is that he was already a millionaire!
She gets on my nerves with her meaningless chatter.

vocabulary.definition: An argument with strong feelings and anger.
vocabulary.example: Raised voices told me that a heated argument was going on next door.
He hit the roof when he saw my report card.

vocabulary.definition: Angry at something thought unfair or insulting.
vocabulary.example: She was indignant at the suggestion that she was lying.
Rude people infuriate me.
Within two minutes of coming off the air, we were inundated with phone calls from irate listeners.
His constant whistling irritates me.
When she finds out that you told him, she'll be livid.
vocabulary.note: Normally after a linking verb in this sense.

vocabulary.definition: Unwilling to do something, often because of anger.
vocabulary.example: I am in no mood to argue!

vocabulary.definition: A sudden strong expression of emotion, often anger.
vocabulary.example: What was the reason for her sudden outburst?

vocabulary.definition: A tendency to become angry easily.
vocabulary.example: He's got a very quick temper, so be careful what you say to him.
vocabulary.note: Not a fast temper in this collocation.

vocabulary.example: I'm sick and tired of your excuses!
vocabulary.note: Follow of with a noun or -ing form.

vocabulary.definition: Show uncontrolled anger, often by crying or shouting.
vocabulary.example: Whenever Tom didn't get his own way, he would throw a tantrum.
I'm sorry I've been so touchy lately.

vocabulary.definition: Very angry and ready to protest.
vocabulary.example: Local people are up in arms about the government's proposal to build a road through the village green.

vocabulary.definition: A person regarded as different or a disappointment in a family.
vocabulary.example: I've always been the black sheep of the family. My father, mother and sister are all lawyers. Me? I'm a rock singer.
She's as blind as a bat without her glasses.

vocabulary.definition: For a very long time, usually with little result.
vocabulary.example: You can ask till the cows come home, but I won't tell you.
vocabulary.note: Also until the cows come home.

vocabulary.definition: A person whose abilities or plans are little known.
vocabulary.example: Sean is a dark horse, a bit of a mystery.
I've been dogged by ill health ever since I left university.
I've known Tom for donkey's years.

vocabulary.definition: Lower your head or body to avoid something.
vocabulary.example: If he hadn't ducked, the ball would have hit him square in the face.

vocabulary.definition: Criticism or trouble that has no effect on someone.
vocabulary.example: His criticisms are like water off a duck's back.
vocabulary.note: Usually like water off a duck’s back.

vocabulary.example: His proposal sounds a bit fishy, so I don't think we should trust him.
The paparazzi hounded her wherever she went.
Julie inherited the lion's share of Uncle Fester's fortune.

vocabulary.definition: Talk for too long in a boring way.
vocabulary.example: She rabbited on for ages.
Sorry I was so ratty this morning. I didn't get much sleep last night.

vocabulary.term: have a whale of a time
vocabulary.example: The kids had a whale of a time.

vocabulary.definition: A search unlikely to achieve anything.
vocabulary.example: Looking for him would be a wild goose chase.

vocabulary.definition: Avoid a duty through clever excuses.
vocabulary.example: He wormed his way out of the work again!
vocabulary.note: Follow of with a noun or -ing form.

exerciseGroups.title: Exercise 1 · Choose the correct item
exerciseGroups.instruction: Choose from the four original alternatives. Use the lesson reference if you need a reminder.

questions.prompt: Angry? I was absolutely ___ when our appointment was cancelled for the third time.
questions.explanation: Livid expresses very strong anger and fits absolutely.
questions.hint: Look at the lesson reference beside the question and read the whole sentence.

questions.prompt: The reason why he gets into trouble so often is that he has a ___ temper.
questions.explanation: The document’s collocation is a quick temper.
questions.hint: Look at the lesson reference beside the question and read the whole sentence.

questions.prompt: What I find most ___ about it is that he didn't even have the decency to say that he was sorry.
questions.explanation: Galling describes something annoying because it seems unfair or wrong.
questions.hint: Look at the lesson reference beside the question and read the whole sentence.

questions.prompt: George wasn't in a particularly good mood, but then he is always a bit ___ in the morning.
questions.explanation: Crotchety describes an irritable, bad-tempered mood.
questions.hint: Look at the lesson reference beside the question and read the whole sentence.

questions.prompt: Like many children of his age, he is prone to throwing a(n) ___.
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is throw a tantrum.
questions.hint: Look at the lesson reference beside the question and read the whole sentence.

questions.prompt: Mum will hit the ___ when she finds out that you've burnt a hole in her new sofa.
questions.explanation: Hit the roof means become very angry.
questions.hint: Look at the lesson reference beside the question and read the whole sentence.

questions.prompt: How much longer do we have to wait? This is starting to get on my ___.
questions.explanation: Get on someone’s nerves means annoy someone.
questions.hint: Look at the lesson reference beside the question and read the whole sentence.

questions.prompt: “I’m ___ to listen to your pathetic excuses,” she said.
questions.explanation: In no mood takes to + verb. Sick and tired takes of.
questions.hint: Look at the lesson reference beside the question and read the whole sentence.

questions.prompt: Stop that tapping, will you? I'm trying to concentrate and it is driving me up the ___.
questions.explanation: Drive someone up the wall means annoy them intensely.
questions.hint: Look at the lesson reference beside the question and read the whole sentence.

questions.prompt: The whole country is up in ___ about the new tax the government has put on books.
questions.explanation: Up in arms describes an angry reaction and readiness to protest.
questions.hint: Look at the lesson reference beside the question and read the whole sentence.

questions.prompt: It was so embarrassing. We were in the middle of a crowded restaurant when they suddenly had a ___ row.
questions.explanation: The expression taught in the document is a blazing row. Heated row is also possible in English, so either is accepted here.
questions.hint: Look at the lesson reference beside the question and read the whole sentence.

exerciseGroups.title: Exercise 2 · Animal words
exerciseGroups.instruction: Complete the sentences with a word formed from an animal in the lesson. The picture clues are represented as an animal-word bank; change the form when needed. Example 0: “I’ve known them for donkey’s years.”

questions.prompt: Throughout his playing career he was ___ by injury.
questions.explanation: Use the verb dog in the passive expression be dogged by.
questions.hint: You may need a verb ending, a plural, or a possessive ending.

questions.prompt: He said we could double our money in two days? It sounds a bit ___ to me.
questions.explanation: Fishy means suspicious.
questions.hint: You may need a verb ending, a plural, or a possessive ending.

questions.prompt: At first, the criticism he got in the press used to affect him, but now it's like water off a ___ back.
questions.explanation: Include the possessive ending: duck’s.
questions.hint: You may need a verb ending, a plural, or a possessive ending.

questions.prompt: Of course she didn't see you. She's as blind as a ___.
questions.explanation: The comparison is as blind as a bat.
questions.hint: You may need a verb ending, a plural, or a possessive ending.

questions.prompt: Did we enjoy the party? We most certainly did. We had a ___ of a time.
questions.explanation: A whale of a time means a very enjoyable time.
questions.hint: You may need a verb ending, a plural, or a possessive ending.

questions.prompt: You can sit there and argue till the ___ come home, but I'm not changing my mind.
questions.explanation: The fixed expression uses the plural cows.
questions.hint: You may need a verb ending, a plural, or a possessive ending.

questions.prompt: If I hadn't ___, the ball would have hit me square between the eyes.
questions.explanation: After had not, use the past participle ducked.
questions.hint: You may need a verb ending, a plural, or a possessive ending.

questions.prompt: Unlike the other players in the semi-finals, Popov is a bit of a dark ___.
questions.explanation: A dark horse is a person little is known about.
questions.hint: You may need a verb ending, a plural, or a possessive ending.

questions.prompt: We're getting nowhere! This is a wild ___ chase.
questions.explanation: Only the missing word goose is needed; chase is already in the sentence.
questions.hint: You may need a verb ending, a plural, or a possessive ending.

questions.prompt: It's only fair. It was his idea, so he should get the ___ share of the profits.
questions.explanation: Include the possessive ending: lion’s.
questions.hint: You may need a verb ending, a plural, or a possessive ending.

questions.prompt: Ted has always been the black ___ of the family. His parents are lawyers, his two brothers are doctors, while he dropped out of school at 15.
questions.explanation: The expression is the black sheep of the family.
questions.hint: You may need a verb ending, a plural, or a possessive ending.

questions.prompt: You're not going to ___ your way out of doing the washing-up this time.
questions.explanation: Worm your way out of means avoid a duty.
questions.hint: You may need a verb ending, a plural, or a possessive ending.

questions.prompt: It was a nightmare. She ___ on about her job for hours!
questions.explanation: Use the past tense of rabbit on.
questions.hint: You may need a verb ending, a plural, or a possessive ending.
